title: 〜は〜です — "X is Y"
explanation: X は Y です means "X is Y". は marks the topic, the thing you are talking about, and here it is said "wa", not "ha"; です at the end is the polite "is / am / are" and never changes for I, you or they. When the topic is obvious, leave it out: がくせいです alone means "I'm a student." Put さん after other people's names but never after your own, and call your own wife and husband つま and おっと, but someone else's おくさん and ごしゅじん. Two look-alikes come later: も replaces は to mean "too", and が also marks a subject but puts the spotlight on it.

title: 〜ですか — asking questions
explanation: Put か at the end of a です sentence and it becomes a question; the word order stays the same, and か does the job of the question mark. Answer with はい or いいえ, or with そうです ("that's right") and ちがいます ("no, that's not right"). To ask "what" or "who", put なん / なに or だれ exactly where the answer will go: しごとは なんですか → しごとは せんせいです. This is the polite way to ask; between partners a rising voice without か comes later with casual speech. Don't mix it up with か between two nouns, which means "or".

title: 〜の〜 — "X's Y"
explanation: の links two nouns, and the first one describes the second: わたしの かさ is "my umbrella", おっとの かばん is "my husband's bag". It also tells where something is from or what kind it is: にほんの くるま (a Japanese car), にほんごの せんせい (a teacher of Japanese). Ask "whose?" with だれの, and drop the second noun when it is obvious: わたしのです means "It's mine." の works the same in polite and casual speech. Later you will meet two other jobs for の: "the red one" and turning a verb into a noun (〜のが すき).

title: これ・それ・あれ — "this, that, that over there"
pattern: これ・それ・あれ・どれ／この〜・その〜・あの〜・どの〜
explanation: これ (this), それ (that) and あれ (that over there) stand on their own: これは なんですか. この, その, あの and どの always need a noun right after them: この かさ, その かばん. Distance is about you and your listener: これ is near you, それ is near your listener, and あれ is away from you both; どれ and どの ask "which?". The same words work in polite and casual speech. Places use the matching set ここ / そこ / あそこ, and "this kind of" uses こんな; both come later.

title: 〜じゃないです — "X is not Y"
pattern: 〜じゃないです・〜ではありません
explanation: To say "X is not Y", swap です for じゃないです: がくせいじゃないです means "I'm not a student." You will also see ではありません and じゃありません; they mean the same but sound more formal, so recognise them and use じゃないです in everyday polite talk. A quick "no" to a yes/no question is いいえ、ちがいます ("No, that's not right"), or いいえ plus the じゃないです sentence. This is for nouns: adjectives make their negative in their own way, the past "wasn't" is じゃなかったです, and the casual ない form comes later.

title: 〜も — "too, also"
explanation: も means "too" or "also" and takes the place of は (or が and を): わたしも がくせいです is "I'm a student too." With a negative it means "not … either": わたしも いしゃじゃないです. Two もs give "both A and B": きょうも あしたも やすみです. Particles like に and で stay in front of it (にも, でも), and it works the same in polite and casual speech. Use plain は, not も, when the second thing is different: おっとは いしゃです。わたしは せんせいです.

title: 〜ね・〜よ — "right?" and "you know"
explanation: ね at the end asks your listener to agree, or shares a feeling you both have: おいしいですね is "It's good, isn't it?" よ tells them something you think they don't know yet: たかいですよ is "It's expensive, you know." Together, よね checks something you are fairly sure of ("…, right?"), and そうですね is the usual way to agree. Both work in polite and casual speech, but go easy on よ with your partner: a lot of it can sound pushy, while ね sounds warm.

title: いくらですか — numbers and prices
pattern: いくらですか・〜{円|えん}です
explanation: Japanese counts in blocks: じゅう (10), ひゃく (100), せん (1,000) and まん (10,000), so 12,000 is いちまん にせん, "one ten-thousand, two thousand". Some combinations change sound: さんびゃく (300), ろっぴゃく (600), はっぴゃく (800), さんぜん (3,000), はっせん (8,000), and 10,000 is always いちまん. Add えん for yen, and ask the price with いくらですか, the polite shop question. Counting objects (ひとつ, ふたつ…) uses a different set of numbers, which comes soon.

title: 〜ます・〜ません — polite verbs
explanation: Polite verbs end in ます, and their negative ends in ません: たべます (eat, will eat), たべません (don't eat, won't eat). Japanese has no separate future tense, so the same form covers "I eat" and "I'll eat"; time words like きょう and あした make it clear. Use ます forms with anyone you aren't close to; with your partner you will later switch to the shorter dictionary form (たべる). For now learn these verbs as whole words: the past (ました) comes soon, and verb groups come with the dictionary form.

title: ここ・そこ・あそこ — "here, there, over there"
pattern: ここ・そこ・あそこ・どこ
explanation: ここ (here), そこ (there, near you) and あそこ (over there) are the place words of the こ・そ・あ set, and どこ asks "where?": トイレは どこですか → あそこです. As with これ and それ, そこ is near your listener and あそこ is away from you both. Shop and hotel staff often use the politer こちら ("here, this way") and どちら ("where, which way"). The words are the same in polite and casual speech; don't mix up ここ (a place) with これ (a thing) or こんな (this kind of), and "there is a … here" comes later with あります and います.

title: 〜を — the thing you act on
explanation: を (said "o") marks the thing an action is done to, and it comes right before the verb: コーヒーを のみます (I drink coffee). The usual order is person は, then thing を, then the verb at the end. In relaxed talk with your partner を is often dropped (コーヒー のむ？), but keep it when you speak politely. One trap for later: すき ("like") takes が, not を.

title: ひとつ・ふたつ — counting things
pattern: ひとつ・ふたつ・みっつ…いくつ
explanation: For everyday objects Japanese has its own set of numbers: ひとつ, ふたつ, みっつ, よっつ, いつつ, むっつ, ななつ, やっつ, ここのつ, とお, and いくつ asks "how many?". The number usually comes after the thing and its particle, right before the verb: たまごを ふたつ かいます (I'll buy two eggs). These words work in polite and casual speech and stop at とお (10). Use them for things, not for people (ひとり, ふたり) or prices (いち, に, さん…); counters like 〜まい come later.

title: 〜じ〜ふん — telling the time
pattern: {何時|なんじ}ですか・〜{時|じ}〜{分|ふん}です
explanation: Add じ for o'clock and ふん or ぷん for minutes: ろくじ, くじ じゅっぷん. Learn the odd hours よじ (4:00), しちじ (7:00) and くじ (9:00), and the minutes that change sound, like いっぷん, さんぷん, ろっぷん and じゅっぷん, while ごふん and にふん keep ふん. はん means "half past", ごぜん and ごご go in front for a.m. and p.m., and ごろ after a time means "around". Ask いま なんじですか (casually, いま なんじ？); "at seven" (with に) comes soon, and dates and lengths of time are separate points.

title: 〜をください — asking for things
pattern: 〜をください・〜をお{願|ねが}いします
explanation: To ask for something in a shop or café, say the thing, then を, then ください: メニューを ください (The menu, please). Put a number after を for how many: コーヒーを ふたつ ください. おねがいします fits the same slot and sounds a little softer; it's the usual way to ask for the bill (おかいけいを おねがいします). Start with すみません to get someone's attention, and when pointing, これ、ください is fine on its own. Both are polite; asking someone to do something (〜て ください) and choosing from a menu (〜に します) come later.

title: 〜に — at a time, to a place
explanation: に marks a point in time: しちじに おきます (I get up at seven), にちようびに (on Sunday). It also marks where you are going with いく, くる and かえる: スーパーに いきます. title: い-adjectives — "it's tasty / it's not tasty"
explanation: い-adjectives end in い and go straight before a noun (おいしい ラーメン) or before です (おいしいです). title: 〜で — where and how
explanation: で marks where an action happens: うちで ばんごはんを たべます (We eat dinner at home). It also marks the tool or way you do something: でんしゃで (by train), はしで (with chopsticks), にほんごで (in Japanese). But where someone simply is, and where you are going, take に (うちに います, かいしゃに いきます); で for "in total" or "the two of us" comes later.

title: あります・います — "there is", "I have"
explanation: To say something is somewhere, use place に, then the thing with が (it marks what exists; が has more uses later), then あります for things (and plans or events) or います for people and animals: れいぞうこに ぎゅうにゅうが あります. The same verbs mean "have": じかんが ありますか (Do you have time?), きょうだいが います. Their negatives are ありません and いません. Being somewhere takes に but doing something somewhere takes で: うちに います, but うちで たべます. These are polite forms; putting a known thing first (かぎは つくえの うえに あります) comes later with position words.

title: 〜と — "and", "with"
explanation: と joins nouns into a complete list, like "and": パンと たまご (bread and eggs). After a person it means "with": おっとと えいがを みました, often with いっしょに added (つまと いっしょに). This と only joins nouns; you can't use it to link verbs or sentences the way English uses "and" (the て-form does that later). It works in polite and casual speech; for a list that isn't complete ("things like…") use や, and for "or" use か.

title: 〜でした — "was" (nouns)
pattern: 〜でした・〜じゃなかったです
explanation: The past of です is でした: きのうは やすみでした (Yesterday was my day off). The past negative is じゃなかったです; the formal ではありませんでした means the same and is worth recognising. Ask "how was it?" with どうでしたか, a good question after a trip or a day apart. This is for nouns and is polite: verbs use ました, and い-adjectives make their past in their own way (〜かったです), which comes later.

title: いつも・よく・ときどき — how often
pattern: いつも・よく・ときどき・あまり〜ません・ぜんぜん〜ません
explanation: These words say how often: いつも (always), よく (often), ときどき (sometimes), たまに (once in a while). あまり (not much) and ぜんぜん (not at all, never) only go with a negative verb: おさけは あまり のみません. They usually sit before the verb or near the start of the sentence, and まいにち and まいあさ work the same way. They are used in polite and casual speech; あまり also softens adjectives (あまり たかくない), which comes later with words like とても.

title: な-adjectives — "quiet, pretty, famous"
explanation: な-adjectives take な before a noun (しずかな カフェ, a quiet café) but drop it before です (しずかです). Their negative works like a noun's: しずかじゃないです, never 〜くないです. Two traps are きれい (pretty, clean) and きらい (dislike): they end in い but are な-adjectives, so it's きれいな へや and きれいじゃないです. These forms are polite with です; compare い-adjectives, which go straight before a noun and use 〜くないです, and the past (でした) comes later.

title: AかB・〜にします — "A or B", "I'll have …"
explanation: か between two nouns means "or": コーヒーか こうちゃ (coffee or tea). Noun + に します means "I'll have…" or "let's go with…" when you choose: わたしは ケーキに します. Ask your partner なにに しますか, or casually なにに する？. Don't confuse this か with the question か at the end of a sentence, or with と, which means "and"; a list that ends in "and so on" uses や.

title: Dictionary form — the plain verb
pattern: {食|た}べる・{飲|の}む・する・{来|く}る
explanation: Every verb has a plain dictionary form, which you use in casual talk with your partner: なに たべる？ (What shall we eat?). To get the ます form, る-verbs drop る (たべる → たべます), う-verbs change their last u sound to i (のむ → のみます), and the two irregular verbs are する → します and くる → きます. Watch the trap: some う-verbs end in る, like かえる (go home), はいる (enter) and きる (cut), so their ます forms are かえります, はいります and きります. Use this plain form only with people you are close to and keep ます for everyone else; full casual speech, with だ and dropped particles, comes a few points later.

title: 〜がすき — likes and dislikes
pattern: 〜が{好|す}きです・〜が{嫌|きら}いです
explanation: すき (like) and きらい (dislike) are な-adjectives, not verbs, so the thing you like takes が, not を: コーヒーが すきです. だいすき means "love" or "really like", and すきな + noun gives "favourite": すきな たべものは なんですか. きらい sounds strong, so people often say あまり すきじゃないです instead. It works politely with です and casually without (すき？ うん、だいすき！); liking activities (〜のが すき) and being good at things (じょうず) come later.

title: 〜かったです・〜でした — "it was …"
explanation: To say something was a certain way, an い-adjective swaps its last い for かったです: たのしい → たのしかったです ("it was fun"), and くないです becomes くなかったです ("it wasn't"). いい is irregular: よかったです and よくなかったです. な-adjectives work like nouns, with でした and じゃなかったです (ひまでした). い-adjectives never take でした, so don't say おいしいでした. These are the polite forms; the casual versions (たのしかった, ひまだった) come with the plain past.

title: 〜へ — "toward"

title: Casual speech — talking with your partner
explanation: With your partner, family and close friends, Japanese drops です and ます. Verbs use the dictionary form (たべます → たべる), い-adjectives just lose です (おいしい, never おいしいだ), and nouns and な-adjectives take だ or nothing at all (やすみだよ). Questions have no か and usually no だ: just let your voice rise at the end (いく？, げんき？), and は and を often drop out too (コーヒーのむ？). Add ね, よ, だよ or だね to sound warm, and keep です and ます for strangers, shop staff and the role-plays.

title: 〜のうえ・〜のなか — where things are
pattern: 〜の{上|うえ}に・〜の{中|なか}に・〜の{隣|となり}に
explanation: To say where something is, name the reference point first and join the position word with の: テーブルのうえ is "on the table" (literally "the table's top"). The common ones are うえ (on, above), した (under), なか (in), まえ (in front of), うしろ (behind), となり (next to), よこ (beside) and ちかく (near). Add に and あります or います: for something new, use が (テーブルのうえにかぎがあります), and for something you're already talking about, use は and put it first (かぎはテーブルのうえにあります). In polite and casual speech alike you can also just end with です or だ: かぎはテーブルのうえです.

title: 〜て — the て-form, "and then"
explanation: The て-form links actions in order, like "and then": おきて、シャワーをあびます ("I get up and take a shower"). The last verb sets the tense and the politeness for the whole sentence, so the て-form itself works in both polite and casual speech. る-verbs swap る for て (たべる → たべて), and う-verbs change by their last sound: う, つ, る → って; む, ぶ, ぬ → んで; く → いて; ぐ → いで; す → して. The odd ones are いく → いって, する → して and くる → きて. Many later patterns are built on it, such as てから ("after doing") and くて for joining adjectives.

title: 〜から〜まで — "from … to"

title: 〜ない — plain "don't"
explanation: The ない-form is the plain way to say "don't" or "won't", used with your partner instead of 〜ません. る-verbs swap る for ない (たべる → たべない); う-verbs change their last sound from u to a and add ない (のむ → のまない), and a final う becomes わ (かう → かわない). The odd ones are する → しない, くる → こない, and ある, which becomes just ない. Adjectives and nouns simply drop です from the polite negative: おいしくない, しずかじゃない, やすみじゃない. Said with a rising voice, ない？ is a friendly invitation: さんぽしない？ ("want to go for a walk?").

title: 〜が — the subject particle
explanation: が marks the subject when it is the new information, especially the answer to "who?" or "which?". Question words like だれ, なに and どれ take が, never は, when they are the subject: だれがつくりましたか ("who made this?"). The answer keeps が, because that is the new part: おっとがつくりました ("my husband did"). は does a different job: it marks a topic you both already know, and the new information comes after it (これはなんですか). Both particles are used in polite and casual speech; more uses of は and が come in later lessons.

title: なんようび・なんにち — days and dates
pattern: {何曜日|なんようび}・〜{月|がつ}〜{日|にち}・いつ
explanation: Days of the week end in ようび: げつようび (Monday), かようび, すいようび, もくようび, きんようび, どようび and にちようび (Sunday), and なんようび asks which day it is. Months are a number plus がつ (watch しがつ, しちがつ and くがつ), and dates are a number plus にち, except the 1st to the 10th, the 14th, the 20th and the 24th, which have their own readings: ついたち, ふつか, みっか, よっか, いつか, むいか, なのか, ようか, ここのか, とおか, じゅうよっか, はつか, にじゅうよっか. Ask "when?" with いつ, and put に after a day or a date when something happens on it (どようびにあいましょう), but not after words like あした or らいしゅう. All of this works the same in polite and casual speech; clock times (〜じ) were a separate lesson.

title: 〜にいく — going to do something

title: 〜から — "because, so"
explanation: Put から after a reason to mean "because" or "so": つかれたから、ねる ("I'm tired, so I'm going to bed"). The reason comes first and the result second, the opposite order to English "because". The reason can be plain or polite (さむいから or さむいですから), but nouns and な-adjectives need だ or です before から (あめだから). Ask why with どうして or casual なんで, and you can answer with just the reason plus から: おもしろいから ("because it's funny"). This is not the から that means "from", which comes after a time or a place; a softer "because", ので, comes later.

title: 〜は〜が〜 — "X has long hair"
explanation: To describe a feature of someone or something, Japanese says "as for X, Y is …": つまはかみがながい (literally "as for my wife, hair is long", so "my wife has long hair"). は marks who or what you're describing, and が marks the part or feature. It's how you talk about places (このみせはパスタがおいしい), the body (あたまがいたい, where わたしは is usually left out) and abilities (わたしはにほんごがすこしわかります). The が here marks the feature, not the answer to "who?" as in the earlier が lesson, and the pattern works the same in polite and casual speech.

title: 〜てもいい — "it's okay to …"
explanation: て-form + もいいですか asks for permission: すわってもいいですか ("may I sit here?", literally "is it fine even if I sit?"). With your partner, drop ですか and let your voice rise: これ、たべてもいい？ Say yes with どうぞ, いいですよ or casual いいよ, and say no gently with ちょっと… . Without the question, it gives permission: ここでまってもいいですよ ("you can wait here"). "Must not" (〜てはいけない) and "don't have to" (〜なくてもいい) look similar but come in their own lessons.

title: 〜とおもう — "I think that …"
explanation: Put とおもう (polite: とおもいます) after a plain-form sentence to give an opinion or a guess: おいしいとおもう ("I think it's tasty"). Nouns and な-adjectives need だ before と: あしたはあめだとおもう. explanation: に also marks the person on the receiving end of an action: ともだちにあう ("meet a friend"), ははにでんわする ("call my mother"). Verbs that use this に include あう, でんわする, メールする, きく (ask), おしえる, おくる and はなす. Compare と, which means doing something together: おっととはなす is "talk with my husband", while おっとにはなす is "tell my husband". It's the same に you know for times and places, now pointed at a person, and it works in polite and casual speech.

title: 〜や〜 — "things like …"
explanation: や joins nouns like と does, but it means the list is just a few examples out of more: にくややさいをかいました ("I bought meat, vegetables and so on"). と gives the complete list: にくとやさい means exactly those two things. You can close a や list with など ("and so on"): パンやたまごなど. や only joins nouns, and listing actions ("I did things like cleaning and shopping") has its own pattern later; both や and など are fine in polite and casual speech.

title: 〜てはいけない — "must not"
pattern: 〜てはいけません・〜ちゃだめ
explanation: て-form + はいけません states a rule, "you must not": ここでしゃしんをとってはいけません ("you mustn't take photos here"). It's strong, so it's for signs, rules and customs (shoes in the house, the onsen, the train) rather than for telling your partner off. In casual speech you'll hear 〜ちゃだめ and 〜じゃだめ (たべちゃだめ！ "don't eat that!"); just recognise those for now. It's the opposite of 〜てもいい ("it's okay to"), and a softer "please don't" (〜ないでください) comes later.

title: 〜のがすき — liking doing things
pattern: 〜のが{好|す}き・〜のが{上手|じょうず}
explanation: To talk about liking or being good at an activity, turn the verb into a thing with の: dictionary form + の + が + すき, as in りょうりするのがすきです ("I like cooking"). The same pattern works with きらい, じょうず (good at), へた (bad at), とくい (my strong point) and にがて (my weak point). Use じょうず about other people and とくい about yourself, because calling yourself じょうず sounds like boasting. To name a hobby, use しゅみは〜ことです ("my hobby is …ing"). This の is not the "X's" の; it just turns an action into a thing, in polite or casual speech.

title: Describing nouns with sentences
explanation: In Japanese, a whole sentence can sit in front of a noun to describe it: きのうみたえいが ("the movie we saw yesterday"). The describing part always comes before the noun and ends in a plain form, even in polite speech: えきのちかくにあるみせ ("the shop near the station"). な-adjectives keep their な (りょうりがじょうずなひと), and the doer inside the describing part takes が, not は: つまがつくったケーキ ("the cake my wife made"). Keep it to one describing sentence per noun for now.

title: 〜けど・〜が — "but"
explanation: けど joins two sentences that pull against each other: たかいけど、おいしい ("it's expensive, but it's good"). が does the same job but sounds more polite and is common in writing: たかいですが、おいしいです. Nouns and な-adjectives need だ or です first: あめだけど. At the very end of a sentence, けど softens it and leaves something unsaid, which is how Japanese politely hints "no": ちょっとたかいですけど… . To start a new sentence with "but", use でも instead; a stronger "even though" (のに) comes later.

title: 〜てから — "after doing"
explanation: て-form + から means "after doing" or "once I've done": ごはんをたべてから、でかけます ("I'll go out after I eat"). The plain て-form just lists actions in order; てから stresses that the first one is finished before the second starts. As with the plain て-form, the last verb sets the tense and the politeness. With a starting point in time it can also mean "since": にほんごをはじめてから ("since I started Japanese"). Don't confuse it with から "because", which follows a plain or polite form (たべたから), not a て-form.

title: 〜という — "say", "called"
explanation: いう means "say", and what was said goes before と. To report what someone said, put a plain form before と: つまはつかれたといいました ("my wife said she was tired"); for someone's exact words, put them in 「」 brackets. いっていました ("was saying") is the everyday way to pass on a message: ともだちはこないといっていました. いう also names things: noun + という + noun means "a … called …" (さくらというみせ), and 〜はにほんごでなんといいますか asks "how do you say … in Japanese?". It uses the same と as とおもう, and it works in polite and casual speech; the casual って comes later.

title: 〜で — "as a group", "in total"
pattern: {二人|ふたり}で・{一人|ひとり}で・{全部|ぜんぶ}で
explanation: で after a number of people or an amount says how many do something together, or what the total is: ふたりでいく ("go, the two of us"), ひとりでかいものにいった ("went shopping by myself"), ぜんぶでいくらですか ("how much is it altogether?"). みんなで ("all together") and じぶんで ("by myself, on my own") work the same way, in polite and casual speech. This is a different job from で for places and tools. It also differs from と, which names the person you're with: つまといく ("go with my wife") vs ふたりでいく ("go as a pair"), and you can use both at once: つまとふたりでいく.

title: 〜ている — states: married, living, knowing
pattern: {結婚|けっこん}している・{住|す}んでいる・{知|し}っている
explanation: Some verbs describe a change that happens in a moment, like getting married, moving somewhere or getting to know something. With these, ている describes the state left afterwards, not an action in progress: けっこんしています means "I'm married", not "I'm getting married". Learn the common ones as set phrases: すんでいます (live), しっています (know), もっています (have), つかれています (be tired), and for clothes きています, はいています and かけています (be wearing). Watch the odd one out: "I don't know" is しりません (casual しらない), not しっていません. In casual speech they shrink the same way as before: しってる？ すんでる.

title: 〜がほしい — "I want (a thing)"
explanation: ほしい means "want" for things: noun + が + ほしい (polite: ほしいです), as in あたらしいスマホがほしいです ("I want a new smartphone"). It's an い-adjective, so it changes like one: ほしかった (wanted), ほしくない (don't want). Use it about yourself, or to ask your partner (たんじょうび、なにがほしい？), but not to state what someone else wants: Japanese avoids speaking directly about other people's feelings. For wanting to do something, use 〜たい instead; wanting someone else to do something (〜てほしい) comes later.

title: 〜よう — casual "let's"
pattern: 〜よう・〜おう（{行|い}こう・{食|た}べよう）
explanation: The plain volitional form is the casual version of 〜ましょう: it means "let's …", and it's what partners say to each other. る-verbs swap る for よう (たべる → たべよう); う-verbs change their last u-sound to o and add う (いく → いこう, のむ → のもう); する → しよう and くる → こよう. Add か for a softer "shall we …?" (〜ようか), and use 〜ようとおもう for "I'm thinking of …". With people you don't know well, stay with 〜ましょう.

title: 〜より・〜のほうが — comparing two things
explanation: Use より for "than". AよりBのほうが + adjective means "B is more … than A": いぬよりねこのほうがすき, "I like cats more than dogs". You can also start with the winner: BはAより〜. To ask which of two, say AとBと、どちらが〜ですか (polite) or AとB、どっちが〜？ (casual), and answer with 〜のほうが. The adjective itself never changes; for "the most" out of three or more, use いちばん instead.

title: 〜ないでください — "please don't"
explanation: To ask someone not to do something, take the plain negative (ない form) and add でください: たべない → たべないでください, "please don't eat it". Between partners, drop ください and just say 〜ないで: しんぱいしないで, "don't worry"; add ね to make it warmer. It's the mirror image of 〜てください ("please do"). Use it for personal requests; for rules ("you must not"), Japanese uses 〜てはいけない.

title: 〜んです — explaining and asking why
explanation: Adding んです to a plain-form sentence turns it into an explanation, like "the thing is …". Use it to explain a situation (あたまがいたいんです, "I've got a headache") or to ask about something you've noticed (どうしたんですか, "what's wrong?"). Nouns and な-adjectives take な first: やすみなんです. Between partners, ask with の？ (なにしてるの？) and explain with んだ or の. Don't put it on every sentence; this sentence-final の is different from the の in のがすき, which turns a verb into a noun.

title: なにか・なにも — "something", "nothing"
explanation: Add か to a question word to make "some-": なにか (something), だれか (someone), どこか (somewhere), いつか (some day). Add も and a negative verb for "no-": なにも〜ない (nothing), だれも〜ない (no one). In questions, なにか means "anything", and the words work the same in polite and casual speech: なにかのみますか to a guest, なにかのむ？ to your partner. Particles like に and と stay in front of も: どこにもいかない, "I'm not going anywhere".

title: 〜とき — "when …"
explanation: とき means "when" or "at the time". Put a plain verb or い-adjective right before it (さむいとき), な-adjectives keep な (ひまなとき), and nouns take の (こどものとき). Use the past before とき when that action is already done at the time: にほんにいったとき, "when we went to Japan", or つかれたとき, "when I get tired". The part before とき stays plain even in polite speech; only the end of the sentence shows politeness (ひまなとき、なにをしますか). For "before" and "after", use まえに and あとで (coming soon), and for "if / once (something happens)", 〜たら comes later.

title: 〜くて・〜で — joining descriptions
explanation: To join two descriptions ("cheap and tasty"), put the first one in its て-form. い-adjectives swap い for くて: やすい → やすくて, and いい becomes よくて. な-adjectives and nouns add で: しずかできれい ("quiet and pretty"), アメリカじんで ("American, and …"). Only the last word shows the tense or politeness, so 〜くて〜です is polite and 〜くて〜かった is past. It works like the verb て-form, which links actions; you'll also hear 〜くて giving a mild reason: いそがしくてつかれた, "I'm tired from being so busy".

title: 〜くなる・〜になる — "become"
explanation: なる means "become". With い-adjectives, change い to く (さむい → さむくなる, "get cold"); with な-adjectives and nouns, add に (げんきになる, "get well"; はるになる, "spring comes"). It's very common in the past, to point out a change: さむくなったね (casual) or さむくなりましたね (polite), "it's gotten cold, hasn't it". To make something change on purpose, use する instead: しずかにして, "please be quiet" (lit. "make it quiet"); the same く and に forms also say how you do things, a later lesson.

title: 〜じかん・かかる — how long it takes
pattern: 〜{時間|じかん}かかる・〜ぐらい
explanation: For lengths of time, add a duration word to the number: 〜ふん/ぷん (minutes), 〜じかん (hours), days (いちにち, then ふつか, みっか … like the dates), 〜しゅうかん (weeks), 〜かげつ (months) and 〜ねん (years). かかる means "to take" (time or money): えきまでじゅっぷんかかる, "it takes ten minutes to the station". Add ぐらい or くらい for "about", and ask with どのくらいかかりますか (casual: どのくらいかかる？). For how often, use 〜に〜かい: いっしゅうかんにさんかい, "three times a week". Don't mix these up with clock time: さんじ is "three o'clock", さんじかん is "three hours".

title: 〜まえに・〜あとで — "before", "after"
explanation: まえに means "before": put the dictionary form in front of it, even when you're telling a story in the past (ねるまえに, "before going to bed"). あとで means "after" and takes the past た form: たべたあとで, "after eating". Nouns take の (しごとのまえに, "before work"; えいがのあとで, "after the movie"), and the end of the sentence decides whether it's polite or casual. 〜てから also means "after", but it stresses doing one thing and then the next, while あとで is looser ("some time after"). For things at the same time, use とき.

title: 〜たり〜たり — "things like … and …"
explanation: To give a few examples of what you do (not the full list), put each verb in the plain past た form, add り, and finish with する: えいがをみたり、かいものをしたりした, "we watched a movie, went shopping, that kind of thing". The tense and politeness go on the final する: 〜たりします (usually do), 〜たりしました (did). The て-form, by contrast, lists actions in order as a complete sequence, and や gives sample nouns rather than actions. You'll also hear a single 〜たりする, which softens one example ("… or something").

title: 〜ほん・〜まい — counters for things
explanation: Japanese counts most things with a counter word after the number. The common ones: 〜ほん for long, thin things and bottles; 〜まい for flat things like paper, tickets and shirts; 〜はい for cups and glasses; 〜こ for small items; 〜ひき for small animals; 〜さつ for books; and 〜かい for times. Some numbers change sound: いっぽん, さんぼん, ろっぽん; いっぱい, さんばい; いっこ, ろっこ; いっぴき, さんびき. The number goes after the thing and its particle, just like ひとつ (ビールをにほんください), and you ask with なん + counter (なんぼん, なんまい). Counters are the same in polite and casual speech, and if one slips your mind, ひとつ, ふたつ … still works for most objects.

explanation: To talk about life experience (things you have or haven't done at some point), use the plain past た form + ことがある: すしをたべたことがある, "I've eaten sushi before". The negative is ことがない, and いちども〜ことがない means "never once". Ask with 〜たことがありますか (polite) or 〜たことある？ (casual, が dropped). Don't use it for recent, specific events like yesterday's dinner; for those, just use the past: きのうすしをたべた.

title: 〜ほうがいい — "you'd better"
pattern: 〜たほうがいい・〜ないほうがいい
explanation: To give advice, use the plain past た form + ほうがいい: はやくねたほうがいい, "you'd better go to bed early". For "you'd better not", use the plain ない form + ほうがいい: のまないほうがいい. On its own it can sound pushy, so soften it with よ or とおもう, and use ほうがいいですよ or ほうがいいとおもいます with people you don't know well. It's advice, not a rule; "must" (〜なければならない) comes later.

title: 〜ので — "because" (softer)
explanation: ので means "because" or "so", like から, but it sounds softer and more considerate, so it's the natural choice for excuses and requests to people you don't know well. The reason comes first: ようじがあるので、さきにかえります, "I have something to do, so I'll head off first". Plain forms usually go before ので, and nouns and な-adjectives take な: あめなので, ひまなので. Between partners, から is more common; ので sounds a little more careful. You can also end a sentence with ので and leave the rest unsaid, as a polite explanation.

title: 〜だけ・〜しか〜ない — "only"
explanation: だけ means "only" or "just" and is neutral: ちょっとだけ, "just a little"; ふたりだけ, "just the two of us". しか also means "only", but it always comes with a negative verb, and it suggests "no more than that", often with a feeling that it's not enough: せんえんしかない, "I've only got 1,000 yen". Both go right after the word they limit. が and を usually drop before だけ and しか, but other particles stay (あなたにだけ, "only to you"), and both words work the same in polite and casual speech.

title: 〜つもり — "I plan to"
explanation: つもり means "intention": a plan you've already made up your mind about. Put the dictionary form before it for "I plan to …" (らいねんにほんにいくつもりです) and the ない form for "I don't plan to …". Ask your partner with 〜つもり？ (or politely 〜つもりですか), and use つもりだった for "I meant to (but didn't)". It's firmer than 〜ようとおもう ("I'm thinking of …"), so save つもり for things you've actually decided. Use つもりです with people you don't know well and just つもり with your partner.

title: 〜って — casual quoting
explanation: って is the casual spoken form of と and という. It reports what someone said: あしたはあめだって, "they say it'll rain tomorrow". It names things: 「さくら」っていうカフェ, "a cafe called Sakura". And it marks a word or person you're asking or talking about: 〜ってなに？ ("what's …?"), 〜ってどういういみ？ ("what does … mean?"). It's everywhere in partner chat and messages, but in polite speech and writing use と and という instead.

title: 〜は — contrast, "as for X …"
explanation: Besides marking the topic, は can show contrast: "X, (unlike Y) …". にくはたべるけど、さかなはたべない (polite: にくはたべますが、さかなはたべません) means "Meat I eat, but fish I don't". It often comes in pairs like that, or alone to hint at an unspoken contrast: ビールはのまない, "beer I don't drink (other things, maybe)". は can follow other particles to contrast them (ここでは, にちようびには), and it often appears in negatives: すきではない. Remember the split: が points at new information or the answer to a question word, while は sets up the topic or a contrast.

title: 〜なければならない — "have to"
pattern: 〜なければならない・〜なきゃ
explanation: To say "have to" or "must", take the ない form, change ない to なければ, and add ならない (polite なりません): おきる → おきなければならない, "I have to get up". なければいけない means the same and is very common in speech. Between partners, the short forms 〜なきゃ and 〜なくちゃ are what you'll actually hear: あしたはやくおきなきゃ. This is a real obligation; for advice use 〜ほうがいい, for "must not" use 〜てはいけない, and "don't have to" (〜なくてもいい) comes later.

title: 〜く・〜に — how you do something
explanation: To say how something is done, turn the adjective into an adverb. い-adjectives change い to く: はやい → はやく ("early, quickly"), and いい → よく ("well"). な-adjectives add に: しずか → しずかに ("quietly"), じょうず → じょうずに ("skillfully"). The adverb goes before the verb: はやくおきる, しずかにはなす. These are the same く and に forms you used with なる, so しずかになる is "become quiet" while しずかにはなす is "talk quietly"; with して they make casual requests: はやくして！ ("hurry up!").

title: 〜でしょう・〜だろう — "probably", "right?"
explanation: でしょう after a plain form means "probably" or "I suppose": あしたははれるでしょう is how a weather forecast sounds. だろう is the plain version, used mostly in your own thoughts and in writing. Said with a rising tone, でしょ？ means "right?", and partners use it all the time: おいしいでしょ？ It's a fairly confident guess; for a weaker "might", かもしれない comes soon.

title: 〜ながら — "while"
explanation: ながら means "while": one person doing two things at the same time. Take the ます form, drop ます, and add ながら: ききます → ききながら, たべます → たべながら. The main action comes last, and the ながら action is the background: おんがくをききながらりょうりする, "I cook while listening to music". Both actions must be done by the same person; for two different people, use 〜ているとき instead. Only the final verb shows politeness, so it fits polite and casual sentences alike.

title: こんな・どんな — "this kind of", "what kind of"
pattern: こんな・そんな・あんな・どんな／こう・そう・ああ・どう
explanation: This set works like これ and ここ, but for kinds and ways. こんな / そんな / あんな / どんな + noun mean "this kind of / that kind of / that kind of (over there) / what kind of": どんなひと？, "what kind of person?". こう / そう / ああ / どう go with verbs for "like this / like that / how": こうかく ("write it like this"), そうおもう ("I think so"), どうやって ("how, by what means"). As before, こ- is near me, そ- is near you or what was just said, あ- is over there or something we both know, and ど- asks. They're used the same way in polite and casual speech, and together with これ and ここ they complete the こそあど table.

title: 〜ことができる — "can do"
explanation: できる means "can" or "be able to". After a noun, use が: りょうりができる, "can cook"; にほんごができる, "can speak Japanese". After a verb, use the dictionary form + ことができる: ここでカードをつかうことができますか. title: 〜てみる — "try doing"
explanation: Add みる ("see") to the て-form to mean "try doing something and see what it's like": たべてみる, "try eating it". It's perfect for suggestions: たべてみて！ ("try it!") or いってみない？ ("want to go and check it out?") with your partner, たべてみてください or いってみませんか with others. This みる is written in kana and changes like the normal verb: 〜てみた, 〜てみたい, 〜てみよう, 〜てみてもいい. It's about testing something out, not about struggling to manage something hard.

title: 〜かもしれない — "might"
explanation: かもしれない means "might" or "maybe": something is possible, but you're not sure. Put it after a plain form: おくれるかもしれない, "I might be late". Nouns and な-adjectives drop だ: あめかもしれない, ひまかもしれない. The polite form is かもしれません, and in casual talk people cut it to just かも. It's less sure than でしょう ("probably"), and unlike 〜みたい ("it seems", coming later) it doesn't need any evidence.

title: あげる・もらう — giving and receiving
explanation: あげる means "give" when the gift goes away from you (or your side) to someone else: つまにはなをあげた, "I gave my wife flowers"; the person who receives takes に. もらう means "receive, get": the receiver is the subject, and the giver takes に or から: おっとにとけいをもらった, "I got a watch from my husband". When someone gives something to you, Japanese doesn't use あげる; that's くれる, which has its own lesson. Both work in polite (あげます, もらいます) and casual forms, and you'll also hear the humble いただく for もらう.

title: Potential form — "can do"
explanation: The potential form is the everyday way to say "can". る-verbs change る to られる (たべる → たべられる; in casual speech you'll often hear たべれる), and う-verbs change their last u-sound to an e-sound and add る (のむ → のめる, いく → いける); する becomes できる and くる becomes こられる. The thing you can do often takes が instead of を (にほんごがはなせる), and the new verb works like any る-verb: はなせます, はなせない. 〜ことができる means the same but sounds more formal. The passive (a later lesson) looks like the る-verb potential, so context tells them apart.

title: 〜てしまう — "ended up", "all of it"
explanation: Add しまう to the て-form to say an action is completely finished, or that something happened that you didn't want: さいふをわすれてしまった, "I (went and) forgot my wallet". It often carries a feeling of "oops" or regret, which makes it perfect for apologies. In casual speech てしまう shrinks to ちゃう (たべちゃった), and でしまう becomes じゃう (のんじゃった); in polite speech say てしまいました. Don't mix it up with ておく, which is for doing something on purpose, ahead of time.

title: 〜たら — "if", "when"
explanation: Take the plain past form and add ら to say "if" or "once (this happens)": いえについたら、でんわして, "call me when you get home"; あめだったら, "if it's raining"; さむかったら, "if you're cold". The たら part always happens first, and the second part can be anything, including a request, a wish or "let's"; 〜たらどう？ means "why don't you …?". It is the most general "if" and works in casual and polite speech alike, since the end of the sentence sets the politeness. とき just means "at the time when", ても means "even if", and ば, と and なら are narrower kinds of "if" that come later.

title: くれる — someone gives to me
explanation: くれる also means "give", but only when the gift comes toward you or someone on your side, like your partner or family: つまがネクタイをくれた, "my wife gave me a tie". title: 〜すぎる — "too much"
explanation: Add すぎる to say something is "too …" or that you did something "too much". With verbs, use the ます-stem, the part before ます: たべすぎた, "I ate too much". With い-adjectives drop the final い (たかい → たかすぎる), with な-adjectives just add すぎる (しずかすぎる), and いい becomes よすぎる. すぎる itself works like a る-verb: すぎます and すぎました in polite speech, すぎる, すぎた and すぎない in casual talk, and すぎて to link a reason (からすぎて、たべられない, "it's too spicy to eat"). It usually sounds like a complaint, so you'll hear it after big dinners and in shops.

explanation: Add そう to say how something looks to you, before you know for sure: おいしそう, "that looks delicious". い-adjectives drop the い (おいしい → おいしそう), な-adjectives just add そう (げんきそう), and verbs use the ます-stem (ふりそう, "it looks like it'll rain"); two special ones are いい → よさそう and ない → なさそう. Before a noun it becomes そうな (おいしそうなケーキ), before a verb そうに, and you add だ or です at the end for casual or polite speech. Careful: かわいそう means "poor thing", not "looks cute". This そう is only about appearance; そうだ meaning "I heard" and ようだ meaning "it seems" are separate lessons.

title: 〜てくれる・〜てもらう — favours
pattern: 〜てくれる・〜てもらう・〜てあげる
explanation: Put くれる, もらう or あげる after the て-form to show who is doing a favour for whom. 〜てくれる means someone does something for me (つまがりょうりをつくってくれた), 〜てもらう means I get someone to do it, with that person + に (おっとにてつだってもらった), and 〜てあげる means I do it for someone, which can sound a little showy, so use it with care. To ask your partner for something, say 〜てくれる？, or more politely 〜てもらえますか, and to thank them, say 〜てくれてありがとう. Unlike plain くれる (giving a thing), these are about actions, and they come up constantly between partners.

title: 〜ば — "if"
explanation: ば is another "if", built by changing the verb's last u-sound to e and adding ば (いく → いけば, たべる → たべれば, する → すれば, くる → くれば); い-adjectives change い to ければ (やすければ, and いい → よければ), ない becomes なければ, and nouns use なら instead. Two set phrases are worth learning whole: 〜ばいい, "you just need to …", and どうすればいい？, "what should I do?"; 〜ばよかった means "I wish I had …". ば puts the focus on the condition itself, while たら is the all-purpose "if / when" and と is for things that always happen. It is fine in both casual and polite speech; the end of the sentence sets the politeness.

title: 〜し — "and besides"
explanation: Put し after a plain-form sentence to stack up reasons, like "… and besides …": やすいし、おいしいし、ここにしよう, "it's cheap, it's tasty — let's go with this place". Nouns and な-adjectives take だ before し (あめだし, ひまだし). Often people give just one reason with し and leave the rest unsaid, which sounds softer than から: あしたはやすみだし…, "well, tomorrow's a day off, so …". から gives one clear reason, while し hints that there are others too. In polite speech you can put です or ます before し (やすいですし).

title: 〜そうだ — "I heard that"
explanation: Put そうだ (casual) or そうです (polite) after a full plain-form sentence to pass on something you heard or read: あしたはあめだそうです, "I hear it's going to rain tomorrow", and say where it came from with 〜によると, "according to …". Watch the form in front: the plain form (ふるそうだ) means "I heard", but the ます-stem (ふりそうだ) means "it looks like", which is a different lesson. Between partners people often just use って instead (あしたあめだって), and らしい also means "apparently". ようだ is your own guess from evidence, whereas そうだ simply reports what someone said.

title: 〜ておく — "do in advance"
explanation: おく means "put" or "leave", and after the て-form it says you do something now so that it's ready for later: ホテルをよやくしておく, "I'll book the hotel ahead of time". It can also mean leaving something as it is: まどをあけておいて, "leave the window open". In casual speech ておく shrinks to とく (かっとく, "I'll buy it") and でおく to どく (よんどく); in polite speech say ておきます. Compare てしまう, which is about finishing something or an accident; ておく is always on purpose, with a plan in mind.

title: 〜と — "whenever", "if (naturally)"
explanation: Put と after the dictionary form (or the ない-form) to say that one thing always or automatically leads to another: ボタンをおすと、ドアがあく, "when you press the button, the door opens". It is perfect for giving directions (みぎにまがると、えきがあります), explaining how machines work, and talking about habits and natural facts. The second half must be something that simply happens, so no requests, wishes or "let's"; for those use たら (いえについたら、でんわして). This と comes after a verb or adjective (a noun needs だ first: あめだと), so it isn't the と that means "and" or "with"; ば and なら are the other "if" words. The end of the sentence sets the politeness, so it works in both casual and polite speech.

title: 〜ようになる — "come to be able"
explanation: Add ようになる to the dictionary form or the potential form to describe a gradual change in what you can do or what you usually do: カタカナがよめるようになった, "I've become able to read katakana". It's the perfect way to talk about your own progress, politely with ようになりました or casually with ようになった. For a change in the other direction, use the ない-form with なくなる: ねむれなくなった, "I can't sleep any more". 〜くなる and 〜になる are for adjectives and nouns, while ようになる is for verbs; ようにする, "make a point of doing", is a close cousin you only need to recognise. Don't confuse it with ことにする, which is a one-off decision, not a gradual change.

title: 〜ようだ・〜みたい — "seems"
explanation: Use ようだ, or casual みたい, when you draw a conclusion from what you notice: だれもいないようです, "it seems nobody's here". Put it after a plain-form sentence; nouns take のようだ or just みたい (あめのようだ, あめみたい), and な-adjectives take なようだ or just みたい (ひまみたい). みたい is what you'll hear and say most with your partner, while ようです is more careful and polite. Both also mean "like" in comparisons: ゆめみたい, "like a dream", and before a noun みたいな or のような. Compare そう (how something looks at a glance), そうだ (what you heard) and かもしれない (it's just possible).

title: 〜なくてもいい — "don't have to"
explanation: To say "you don't have to …", take the ない-form, change ない to なくて, and add もいい: いそがなくてもいい, "you don't have to hurry". With your partner the も is often dropped (いそがなくていいよ), and in polite speech you say いいです. It is the opposite of なければならない ("have to"), and the partner of てもいい: てもいい gives permission to do something, なくてもいい gives permission not to. Nouns and な-adjectives use じゃなくてもいい: すぐじゃなくてもいい, "it doesn't have to be right away".

title: 〜なら — "if it's …"
explanation: なら means "if (as you say)" or "if it's about …", and it usually builds on something the other person has just said: きょうとにいくなら、あきがいいよ, "if you're going to Kyoto, autumn is best". Put it straight after a noun (すしなら、あのみせ) or a な-adjective (ひまなら), or after a plain-form verb or い-adjective (さむいなら). It is the natural way to give advice and recommendations, in casual or polite speech. Unlike たら, the なら part doesn't have to happen first: you pick autumn before you go to Kyoto. ば and と are the other "if" words, for general conditions and automatic results.

title: Passive — "was done (to me)"
explanation: The passive form says what was done to someone: う-verbs change the last u-sound to a and add れる (ふむ → ふまれる, いう → いわれる), る-verbs add られる (たべる → たべられる), する becomes される and くる becomes こられる. The person who did it is marked with に: つまにおこられた, "I got told off by my wife". Japanese also uses the passive for things that happen to you and annoy you, even the weather: あめにふられた, "I got caught in the rain". る-verb passives look exactly like the potential form, and the same shape is also used as a polite honorific, so let the context guide you; the causative (させる, "make someone do") is a different form. You only need to recognise passives for now, in casual and polite speech alike.

title: 〜ことにする — "decide to"
explanation: Add ことにする to the dictionary form or the ない-form to say you decide to do (or not to do) something: らいげつひっこすことにした, "we've decided to move next month". You'll mostly hear it in the past, ことにしました or casual ことにした, to report a decision. ことにしている means it's your personal rule or habit: まいあさはしることにしている, "I make a point of running every morning". When a decision is made by others or by circumstances, Japanese says ことになる (ことになった, "it's been decided"); just recognise it for now. Don't confuse it with ようになる, which is a gradual change rather than a decision; にする alone picks a thing (コーヒーにする).

title: 〜ても — "even if"
explanation: Add も to the て-form to say "even if" or "even though": あめがふっても、いきます, "I'll go even if it rains"; い-adjectives become くても (さむくても), and nouns and な-adjectives use でも (あめでも, ひまでも). With a question word it means "no matter …": いくらたべても、ふとらない, "no matter how much I eat, I don't put on weight". Don't confuse it with てもいい ("it's okay to …"), which gives permission. たら says what will happen if something happens, while ても says the result stays the same anyway; のに, coming later, is for frustrating real-life contrasts. It works in casual and polite speech alike.

title: 〜ところ — "about to", "in the middle of", "just did"
explanation: ところ means "point" or "moment", and the verb form in front tells you which moment: dictionary form + ところ is "just about to" (いまでるところ, "I'm just about to leave"), ている + ところ is "right in the middle of" (たべているところ), and た + ところ is "have just done" (いまついたところ, "I've just arrived"). It's perfect for quick messages to your partner. Add です for polite speech or だ in casual speech, or drop it altogether in a text. ている on its own just says something is going on; ているところ stresses "right at this very moment".

title: Honorific and humble verbs
pattern: いらっしゃる・{召|め}し{上|あ}がる・いただく・{申|もう}す
explanation: Staff in shops, hotels and on the phone use special respectful verbs, and you'll hear them every time you travel in Japan. Honorific verbs lift up the other person: いらっしゃる (be, come, go), めしあがる (eat, drink), おっしゃる (say), なさる (do), ごらんになる (look) and くださる (give me). Humble verbs lower yourself: いただく (receive, eat), まいる (come, go), もうす (say, be called), おる (be) and いたす (do). Ordinary verbs can also become honorific with お〜になる (おまちになる) or humble with お〜する (おもちします, "let me carry that"), and passive-looking forms like こられる are sometimes used as light honorifics too. You only need to recognise these, alongside set phrases like いらっしゃいませ; when you speak, ordinary ます-forms are perfectly polite.

title: 〜か — questions inside sentences
explanation: To tuck a question inside a bigger sentence, end the question part with か: なんじにはじまるかわからない, "I don't know what time it starts". If the question has no question word (a yes/no question), use かどうか, "whether or not": くるかどうかきいてみる, "I'll ask whether she's coming". Use the plain form before か, but drop だ after nouns and な-adjectives: ほんとうかどうか, "whether it's true". The bigger verb is usually わからない, しらない, おぼえていない, きいてみる or おしえて. It works in casual and polite speech; just make the last verb polite (わかりません).

title: 〜てほしい — "I want you to"
explanation: On its own, ほしい means you want a thing (なにがほしい？); after the て-form it means you want someone else to do something: もっとはなしてほしい, "I want you to talk to me more". The person you want to act takes に: おっとにてつだってほしい, "I want my husband to help". For "I don't want you to …", use the ない-form + でほしい: しんぱいしないでほしい. Said straight to someone it can sound demanding, so for everyday requests the softer 〜てくれる？ or 〜てもらえる？ usually works better. Add です for polite speech (〜てほしいです), or soften it with な or んだけど with your partner.

title: 〜のに — "even though"
explanation: のに links two facts when the second is unexpected, disappointing or annoying: やくそくしたのに、こなかった, "even though he promised, he didn't come". Use the plain form before のに, but nouns and な-adjectives take な (やすみなのに, ひまなのに). At the end of a sentence のに shows regret or a mild complaint: いっしょにいきたかったのに, "and I really wanted to go with you". けど is a neutral "but", and ても is "even if" about things that may happen, while のに is about real facts and carries feeling. It works in casual and polite speech, but because it sounds like a complaint, use it gently with your partner!

title: Causative — "make / let someone"
explanation: The causative form says someone makes or lets another person do something. Build it from the ない-form stem: う-verbs change the last u-sound to a and add せる (いく → いかせる, まつ → またせる), る-verbs add させる (たべる → たべさせる), する becomes させる and くる becomes こさせる. The person who is made or allowed to act usually takes に: こどもにやさいをたべさせる, "I make the kids eat vegetables". The set phrase 〜させてください means "please let me …" (はらわせてください, "let me pay"), and おまたせしました, "sorry to keep you waiting", comes from the same form. Don't mix it up with the passive (〜れる・〜られる, "was done to me"); you only need to recognise causatives for now.
